claim: The World Mortality Dataset collected weekly, monthly, or quarterly all-cause mortality data from 103 countries and territories.
source: To fill this gap, we have collected weekly, monthly, or quarterly all-cause mortality data from 103 countries and territories, openly available as the regularly updated World Mortality Dataset.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number and types of countries included in the dataset.

claim: In Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, and Mexico, excess mortality was above 50% of the expected annual mortality.
source: We found that in several worst-affected countries (Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Mexico) the excess mortality was above 50% of the expected annual mortality (Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Mexico) or above 400 excess deaths per 100,000 population (Peru, Bulgaria, North Macedonia, Serbia).
evidence: The manuscript presents computed excess mortality percentages for these countries based on the dataset analysis.

claim: Peru, Bulgaria, North Macedonia, and Serbia had above 400 excess deaths per 100,000 population.
source: We found that in several worst-affected countries (Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Mexico) the excess mortality was above 50% of the expected annual mortality (Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Mexico) or above 400 excess deaths per 100,000 population (Peru, Bulgaria, North Macedonia, Serbia).
evidence: The manuscript presents computed excess mortality rates per 100,000 population for these countries.

claim: In Australia and New Zealand, mortality during the pandemic was below the usual level, presumably due to social distancing measures decreasing the non-COVID infectious mortality.
source: At the same time, in several other countries (e.g. Australia and New Zealand) mortality during the pandemic was below the usual level, presumably due to social distancing measures decreasing the non-COVID infectious mortality.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing negative excess mortality and provides a speculative explanation based on social distancing effects.

claim: Some countries have been substantially underreporting their COVID-19 deaths, including Nicaragua, Russia, and Uzbekistan.
source: Furthermore, we found that while many countries have been reporting the COVID-19 deaths very accurately, some countries have been substantially underreporting their COVID-19 deaths (e.g. Nicaragua, Russia, Uzbekistan), by up to two orders of magnitude (Tajikistan).
evidence: The manuscript compares excess mortality to official COVID-19 death counts to identify underreporting.

claim: Tajikistan underreported COVID-19 deaths by up to two orders of magnitude.
source: Furthermore, we found that while many countries have been reporting the COVID-19 deaths very accurately, some countries have been substantially underreporting their COVID-19 deaths (e.g. Nicaragua, Russia, Uzbekistan), by up to two orders of magnitude (Tajikistan).
evidence: The manuscript calculates an undercount ratio of 100 for Tajikistan based on excess mortality versus official counts.

claim: Excess mortality is defined as the increase in all-cause mortality relative to the expected mortality.
source: Excess mortality, defined as the increase in all-cause mortality relative to the expected mortality, is widely considered as a more objective indicator of the COVID-19 death toll.
evidence: The manuscript provides a standard definition used in epidemiology.

claim: Excess mortality is widely considered as a more objective indicator of the COVID-19 death toll than reported cases and deaths.
source: Excess mortality, defined as the increase in all-cause mortality relative to the expected mortality, is widely considered as a more objective indicator of the COVID-19 death toll.
evidence: The manuscript cites established scientific consensus on the use of excess mortality.

claim: Reported numbers of COVID-19 cases and deaths can be strongly affected by testing capacity and reporting policy.
source: Comparing the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic between countries or across time is difficult because the reported numbers of cases and deaths can be strongly affected by testing capacity and reporting policy.
evidence: The manuscript draws on established knowledge about limitations of COVID-19 reporting.

claim: Excess mortality has been used to estimate the death toll of pandemics from the Great Plague of London in 1665 to modern influenza pandemics.
source: Excess mortality, defined as the increase of the all-cause mortality over the mortality expected based on historic trends, has long been used to estimate the death toll of pandemics and other extreme events—from the Great Plague of London in 1665 (as described in Boka and Wainer, 2020), to the influenza epidemic in London in 1875 (Farr, 1885; Langmuir, 1976), the XX–XXI century influenza pandemics of 1918, 1957, 1968, 2009 (Murray et al., 2006; Viboud et al., 2005; Viboud et al., 2016; Simonsen et al., 2013) as well as seasonal influenza epidemics (Housworth and Langmuir, 1974), and more recently for example Hurricane Maria in Puerto-Rico in 2016 (Milken Institute, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites historical uses of excess mortality methodology.

claim: EuroStat began collecting total weekly deaths across European countries in April 2020.
source: In April 2020, EuroStat (http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat) began collecting total weekly deaths across European countries, 'in order to support the policy and research efforts related to COVID-19'.
evidence: The manuscript describes when EuroStat started their data collection effort.

claim: The EuroStat dataset covers 36 European countries at the time of writing.
source: At the time of writing, this dataset covers 36 European countries and also contains sub-national (NUTS1–3 regions) data as well as data disaggregated by age groups and by sex for some countries.
evidence: The manuscript reports the coverage of the EuroStat dataset.

claim: The Human Mortality Database started compiling the Short Term Mortality Fluctuations (STMF) dataset in May 2020.
source: In May 2020, the Human Mortality Database (http://mortality.org), a joint effort by the University of California, Berkeley, and Max Planck Institute for Demographic Research (Barbieri et al., 2015), started compiling the Short Term Mortality Fluctuations (STMF) dataset (STMF, 2021; Islam et al., 2021; Németh et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript describes when the STMF dataset was initiated.

claim: The STMF dataset consists of weekly data disaggregated by five age groups and by sex, and contains 35 countries with 2020 data.
source: This dataset consists of weekly data, disaggregated by five age groups and by sex, and currently contains 35 countries with 2020 data.
evidence: The manuscript describes the structure and coverage of the STMF dataset.

claim: The World Mortality Dataset includes 50 countries with weekly data, 51 countries with monthly data, and two countries with quarterly data.
source: This includes 50 countries with weekly data, 51 countries with monthly data, and two countries with quarterly data (Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the breakdown of data types in the dataset and references Figure 1.

claim: The World Mortality Dataset is openly available at https://github.com/akarlinsky/world_mortality and is updated almost daily.
source: The dataset is openly available at https://github.com/akarlinsky/world_mortality and is updated almost daily.
evidence: The manuscript provides the location and update frequency of the dataset.

claim: Statistically significant positive excess mortality was found in 69 out of 103 countries.
source: Our analysis (updated almost daily at https://github.com/dkobak/excess-mortality) showed statistically significant positive excess mortality in 69 out of 103 countries.
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of statistical analysis of the dataset.

claim: The largest excess mortality in absolute numbers was observed in the United States (640,000 by June 6, 2021), Brazil (500,000 by May 31, 2021), Russia (500,000 by April 30, 2021), and Mexico (470,000 by May 23, 2021).
source: In terms of the absolute numbers, the largest excess mortality in our dataset was observed in the United States (640,000 by June 6, 2021; all reported numbers here and below have been rounded to two significant digits), Brazil (500,000 by May 31, 2021), Russia (500,000 by April 30, 2021), and Mexico (470,000 by May 23, 2021) (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents computed excess mortality totals for these countries and references Figure 3.

claim: Australia had −3,700 excess deaths.
source: For example, Australia had −3,700 excess deaths, Uruguay had −2,200 deaths, and New Zealand had −1,900 deaths.
evidence: The manuscript presents computed negative excess mortality values.

claim: Uruguay had −2,200 excess deaths.
source: For example, Australia had −3,700 excess deaths, Uruguay had −2,200 deaths, and New Zealand had −1,900 deaths.
evidence: The manuscript presents computed negative excess mortality values.

claim: New Zealand had −1,900 excess deaths.
source: For example, Australia had −3,700 excess deaths, Uruguay had −2,200 deaths, and New Zealand had −1,900 deaths.
evidence: The manuscript presents computed negative excess mortality values.

claim: In Australia, Uruguay, and New Zealand, the decrease in mortality happened during the southern hemisphere winter season.
source: In these three cases, the decrease in mortality happened during the southern hemisphere winter season (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript observes seasonal patterns in the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Norway had −1,500 excess deaths, with most of this decrease happening during the 2020/21 winter season.
source: Similarly, Norway had −1,500 excess deaths, with most of this decrease happening during the 2020/21 winter season.
evidence: The manuscript presents computed negative excess mortality and observes seasonal patterns.

claim: The highest excess mortality per 100,000 inhabitants was observed in Peru (590).
source: The highest excess mortality per 100,000 inhabitants was observed in Peru (590), followed by some Eastern European and then Latin American countries: Bulgaria (460), North Macedonia (420), Serbia (400), Mexico (360), Ecuador (350), Lithuania (350), Russia (340), etc. (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents normalized excess mortality rates and references Figure 3.

claim: Bulgaria had 460 excess deaths per 100,000 inhabitants.
source: The highest excess mortality per 100,000 inhabitants was observed in Peru (590), followed by some Eastern European and then Latin American countries: Bulgaria (460), North Macedonia (420), Serbia (400), Mexico (360), Ecuador (350), Lithuania (350), Russia (340), etc. (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents normalized excess mortality rates.

claim: The infection-fatality rate (IFR) of COVID-19 is strongly age-dependent.
source: The infection-fatality rate (IFR) of COVID-19 is strongly age-dependent (Levin et al., 2020; O'Driscoll et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites published research on COVID-19 IFR.

claim: The relative increase in mortality (P-score) was highest in Peru (153%), Ecuador (80%), Bolivia (68%), and Mexico (61%).
source: This relative increase, also known as a P-score (Aron and Muellbauer, 2020), was by far the highest in Latin America: Peru (153%), Ecuador (80%), Bolivia (68%), and Mexico (61%) (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents computed P-scores and references Figure 3.

claim: Parts of Peru showed the highest measured seroprevalence level in the world.
source: That the highest relative mortality increase was observed in Peru, is in agreement with some parts of Peru showing the highest measured seroprevalence level in the world (Álvarez-Antonio et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites published seroprevalence data to support the excess mortality findings.

claim: France had an undercount ratio of 0.7.
source: Some countries had ratio below 1, for example 0.7 in France and 0.6 in Belgium, where reporting of COVID deaths is known to be very accurate (Sierra et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript calculates undercount ratios from the data.

claim: Belgium had an undercount ratio of 0.6.
source: Some countries had ratio below 1, for example 0.7 in France and 0.6 in Belgium, where reporting of COVID deaths is known to be very accurate (Sierra et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript calculates undercount ratios from the data.

claim: The undercount ratio in Italy, Spain, Netherlands, and United Kingdom was approximately 1.5 during the first wave but decreased to approximately 1.0 during the second wave.
source: For example, the undercount ratio in Italy, Spain, Netherlands, and United Kingdom was ∼1.5 during the first wave (Figure 4), but decreased to ∼1.0 during the second wave.
evidence: The manuscript observes temporal changes in undercount ratios and references Figure 4.

claim: Several countries showed very accurate reporting of COVID-19 deaths with the undercount ratio being close to 1.0 from the beginning of the pandemic, including Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Slovenia, and Sweden.
source: On the other hand, several countries showed very accurate reporting of the COVID-19 deaths with the undercount ratio being close to 1.0 (Sierra et al., 2020) from the beginning of the pandemic and up until the middle of the second wave (e.g. Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Slovenia, Sweden; Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript analyzes undercount ratios over time and references Figure 4.

claim: Starting from December 2020 and up until March–April 2021, excess deaths were underestimating the COVID-19 deaths in Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Slovenia, and Sweden.
source: However, starting from December 2020 and up until March–April 2021 the excess deaths were underestimating the COVID-19 deaths in all these countries.
evidence: The manuscript observes temporal patterns in the relationship between excess deaths and reported COVID deaths.

claim: The difference between officially reported COVID-19 deaths and excess deaths from week 40 of 2020 until week 15 of 2021, as a fraction of baseline annual deaths, was in the 2.3–5.9% range for Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Slovenia, and Sweden.
source: This difference (computed starting from week 40 of 2020 and until week 15 of 2021), as a fraction of baseline annual deaths, was in the 2.3–5.9% range (Austria: 2.3%, Belgium: 5.9%, France: 4.3%, Germany: 3.9%, Slovenia: 3.5%, Sweden: 5.5%).
evidence: The manuscript calculates the difference between reported COVID deaths and excess deaths for specific countries and time periods.

claim: The 2.3–5.9% difference between reported COVID deaths and excess deaths is in good agreement with the total negative excess deaths observed in Australia, New Zealand, Uruguay, and Norway.
source: This is in good agreement with the total negative excess deaths observed in Australia, New Zealand, Uruguay, and Norway (−2.5%, −5.4%, −6.4%, −3.7%) and coming mainly from the Southern and Northern hemisphere winter months respectively (Kung et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript compares calculated differences across different countries to support an inference.

claim: The highest undercount ratios were found in Tajikistan (100), Nicaragua (51), Uzbekistan (31), Belarus (14), and Egypt (13).
source: We found the highest undercount ratios in Tajikistan (100), Nicaragua (51), Uzbekistan (31), Belarus (14), and Egypt (13) (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript calculates undercount ratios and references Figure 3.

claim: Large undercount ratios strongly suggest purposeful misdiagnosing or underreporting of COVID-19 deaths.
source: Such large undercount ratios strongly suggest purposeful misdiagnosing or underreporting of COVID-19 deaths, as argued by Kobak, 2021a for the case of Russia (undercount ratio 4.5).
evidence: The manuscript infers intentional underreporting from large undercount ratios and cites supporting analysis.

claim: 83 of the countries in the World Mortality Dataset have a death registration coverage rate of 90% and above according to the United Nations Demographic Yearbook.
source: According to the United Nations Demographic Yearbook (UNSD, 2019), 83 of the countries in our dataset have a death registration coverage rate of 90% and above.
evidence: The manuscript cites UN data on death registration coverage.

claim: In the remaining 20 countries in the dataset, death registration coverage is either estimated to be below 90% or no estimate exists at all.
source: In the remaining 20 countries, coverage is either estimated to be below 90% (e.g. Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia) or no estimate exists at all (Kosovo, Taiwan, Transnistria).
evidence: The manuscript reports limitations in death registration coverage for some countries.

claim: The early pre-outbreak 2020 data for all countries in the dataset matched the baseline obtained from the historic 2015–2019 data.
source: Importantly, the early pre-outbreak 2020 data for all countries in our dataset matched the baseline obtained from the historic 2015–2019 data, indicating that the data are self-consistent and the excess mortality estimates are not inflated.
evidence: The manuscript validates the consistency of the data by comparing early 2020 to historical baselines.

claim: Countries that implemented stringent lockdown and social distancing measures in the absence of COVID-19 community spread, such as Australia, New Zealand, and Uruguay, showed a clear winter-season decrease in all-cause mortality, likely due to reduced influenza transmission.
source: Indeed, countries that implemented stringent lockdown and social distancing measures in the absence of COVID-19 community spread, such as Australia, New Zealand, and Uruguay, showed a clear winter-season decrease in all-cause mortality, likely due to reduced influenza transmission (Kung et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript observes patterns in the data and provides a speculative explanation supported by citation.

claim: Influenza suppression alone can lead to a decrease of annual mortality by 3–6%.
source: Here, using these three countries as well as some of the European data, we estimated that the influenza suppression alone can lead to a decrease of annual mortality by 3–6%.
evidence: The manuscript estimates the effect of influenza suppression based on data from multiple countries.

claim: In South Africa, lockdowns have noticeably decreased toddler mortality (0–4 years).
source: For example, in South Africa, lockdowns have noticeably decreased toddler mortality (0–4 years) (Bradshaw et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites published research on the effect of lockdowns on toddler mortality.

claim: Traffic accident fatalities have decreased in the European Union and the Western Balkans.
source: Traffic accident fatalities have decreased in the European Union and the Western Balkans (European Commission, 2021; Transport Community, 2021) but have increased in the United States (National Safety Council, 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites reports on traffic accident trends.

claim: Traffic accident fatalities have increased in the United States.
source: Traffic accident fatalities have decreased in the European Union and the Western Balkans (European Commission, 2021; Transport Community, 2021) but have increased in the United States (National Safety Council, 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites reports on traffic accident trends.

claim: Homicides have increased in the United States and Germany.
source: Homicides have increased in the United States (Arthur and Asher, 2020; Faust et al., 2021) and Germany (Federal Criminal Police Office, 2021) but have decreased in Peru (Calderon-Anyosa and Kaufman, 2021), South Africa (Bradshaw et al., 2021), and France (Ministry of the Interior, 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites reports on homicide trends.

claim: Homicides have decreased in Peru, South Africa, and France.
source: Homicides have increased in the United States (Arthur and Asher, 2020; Faust et al., 2021) and Germany (Federal Criminal Police Office, 2021) but have decreased in Peru (Calderon-Anyosa and Kaufman, 2021), South Africa (Bradshaw et al., 2021), and France (Ministry of the Interior, 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites reports on homicide trends.

claim: Suicides have first decreased and then increased in Japan, particularly in females.
source: Suicides have first decreased and then increased in Japan, particularly in females (Kurita et al., 2021; Tanaka and Okamoto, 2021; Black and Kutcher, 2021), have decreased in the United States (Ahmad and Anderson, 2021; Faust et al., 2021), and in a study of 21 countries were found to have decreased in half of them and remained unchanged in the rest (Pirkis et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on suicide trends.

claim: Suicides have decreased in the United States.
source: Suicides have first decreased and then increased in Japan, particularly in females (Kurita et al., 2021; Tanaka and Okamoto, 2021; Black and Kutcher, 2021), have decreased in the United States (Ahmad and Anderson, 2021; Faust et al., 2021), and in a study of 21 countries were found to have decreased in half of them and remained unchanged in the rest (Pirkis et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on suicide trends.

claim: In a study of 21 countries, suicides were found to have decreased in half of them and remained unchanged in the rest.
source: Suicides have first decreased and then increased in Japan, particularly in females (Kurita et al., 2021; Tanaka and Okamoto, 2021; Black and Kutcher, 2021), have decreased in the United States (Ahmad and Anderson, 2021; Faust et al., 2021), and in a study of 21 countries were found to have decreased in half of them and remained unchanged in the rest (Pirkis et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites a multi-country study on suicide trends.

claim: In the United States, deaths from drug overdoses and unintentional injuries have increased.
source: In the United States, deaths from drug overdoses and unintentional injuries have increased (Faust et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on drug overdose and unintentional injury trends.

claim: In all cited studies, the combined effect of all changes in the frequency of unnatural deaths did not exceed approximately 1% of the baseline annual mortality.
source: However, importantly, in all cited studies the combined effect of all changes in the frequency of unnatural changes did not exceed ∼1% of the baseline annual mortality, meaning that factor (D) plays only a minor role in excess mortality.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes findings from multiple cited studies to draw a conclusion.

claim: Lockdown and social distancing measures on their own decrease the death rate, at least in short-term.
source: Together, the evidence suggests that the contribution of factor (C) is negative and contribution of factor (D) is small in comparison, so we believe that lockdown and social distancing measures on their own decrease — and not increase — the death rate, at least in short-term.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the presented evidence about the effect of lockdowns.

claim: Whenever COVID deaths are counted perfectly, they should exceed the excess mortality, leading to undercount ratio below 1.
source: In other words, we speculate that whenever COVID deaths are counted perfectly, they should exceed the excess mortality, leading to undercount ratio below 1.
evidence: The manuscript presents a speculative hypothesis based on the analysis.

claim: Belgium, France, and Germany had undercount ratios of 0.6, 0.7, and 0.4, respectively.
source: This is indeed what we observed in several countries with strong COVID-19 outbreaks but accurate accounting of COVID deaths, for example Belgium, France, and Germany (undercount ratios 0.6, 0.7, and 0.4, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript presents calculated undercount ratios to support the speculation.

claim: Summing up the excess mortality estimates across all countries in the dataset gives 4.0 million excess deaths.
source: Summing up the excess mortality estimates across all countries in our dataset gives 4.0 million excess deaths.
evidence: The manuscript aggregates excess mortality estimates across all countries.

claim: Summing up the official COVID-19 death counts across all countries in the dataset gives 2.9 million deaths, corresponding to a global undercount ratio of 1.4.
source: In contrast, summing up the official COVID-19 death counts gives 2.9 million deaths, corresponding to the global undercount ratio of 1.4.
evidence: The manuscript aggregates official death counts and calculates a global undercount ratio.

claim: The Economist estimated 7–13 million excess deaths worldwide in May 2021, which was 2–4 times higher than the world's official COVID-19 death count at the time (3.5 million).
source: Using a statistical model to predict the excess mortality in the rest of the world based on the existing data from our dataset, The Economist in May 2021 estimated 7–13 million excess deaths worldwide (The Economist, 2021), which was 2–4 times higher than the world's official COVID-19 death count at the time (3.5 million).
evidence: The manuscript cites The Economist's modeling estimates.

claim: The dataset has been incorporated into the excess mortality trackers by Our World in Data, The Economist, and the Financial Times.
source: After the initial release of our manuscript, the dataset has been incorporated into the excess mortality trackers by Our World in Data (Giattino et al., 2020), The Economist, and the Financial Times.
evidence: The manuscript reports the adoption of the dataset by major organizations.

claim: The World Mortality Dataset adds 59 additional countries beyond those covered by EuroStat and STMF.
source: Our dataset builds upon the EuroStat and the STMF datasets, adding 59 additional countries — many more than any previous media or academic effort.
evidence: The manuscript describes the contribution of the dataset relative to existing datasets.

claim: EuroStat and STMF together cover 44 countries.
source: Both datasets are regularly updated and have considerable overlap, covering together 44 countries.
evidence: The manuscript reports the combined coverage of existing datasets.

claim: The 2020–2021 data are often preliminary and subject to backward revisions.
source: An important caveat is that recent (2020 and 2021) data are often preliminary and subject to backwards revisions, which we incorporate into our dataset.
evidence: The manuscript describes a limitation of the data.

claim: The baseline mortality for 2020 was predicted using historical data from 2015 to 2019, accounting for linear trend and seasonal variation.
source: For each country, we predicted the 'baseline' mortality in 2020 based on the 2015–2019 data (accounting for linear trend and seasonal variation; see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodology used for baseline estimation.

claim: Excess mortality was obtained as the difference between the actual 2020–2021 all-cause mortality and the baseline.
source: We then obtained excess mortality as the difference between the actual 2020–2021 all-cause mortality and our baseline (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the calculation method for excess mortality.

claim: The total excess mortality was computed from the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic (from March 2020).
source: For each country, we computed the total excess mortality from the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic (from March 2020) (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the time period used for total excess mortality calculation.

claim: 4000 deaths were subtracted from the excess mortality estimates for Armenia and Azerbaijan to account for the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh war.
source: We subtracted 4000 from the excess mortality estimates for Armenia and Azerbaijan to account for the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh war.
evidence: The manuscript describes an adjustment made to the data to account for war casualties.

claim: Weeks 32–34 were excluded from the excess mortality calculation in Belgium, Netherlands, France, Luxembourg, and Germany to account for an August 2020 heat wave.
source: Another correction was done for Belgium, Netherlands, France, Luxembourg, and Germany, where our data show a peak of excess deaths in August 2020, not associated with COVID-19 (see below and Figure 4) and likely corresponding to a heat wave (Fouillet et al., 2006; Fouillet et al., 2008; Flynn et al., 2005). We excluded weeks 32–34 from the excess mortality calculation in these five countries.
evidence: The manuscript describes an adjustment made to account for a non-COVID event.

claim: The data were obtained from the websites of National Statistics Offices.
source: Briefly, we obtained the data from the websites of National Statistics Offices (NSOs).
evidence: The manuscript describes the data collection methodology.

claim: If data could not be located on NSO websites, the authors contacted the NSO for guidance.
source: If we were unable to locate the data ourselves, we contacted the NSO for guidance.
evidence: The manuscript describes the data collection methodology.

claim: The World Mortality Dataset includes data from 2015 onward.
source: We collected the all-cause mortality data from 103 countries and territories from 2015 onward into the openly available World Mortality Dataset.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal scope of the dataset.

claim: The authors are committed to keep maintaining the World Mortality Dataset for the entire duration of the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: We are committed to keep maintaining this dataset for the entire duration of the COVID-19 pandemic.
evidence: The manuscript states the authors' commitment to ongoing data maintenance.
